title: Microbial Genetics
source_note: Standard NUC-aligned Nigerian university 200L Microbial Genetics curriculum: bacterial chromosome and plasmid organisation, DNA replication, mutation and DNA repair, gene expression and its regulation (operon model), and the three classical mechanisms of bacterial gene transfer -- transformation, transduction and conjugation. This is the classical-genetics foundation that the later Molecular Biology course builds on with the biochemical/biotechnological detail.

questions.question: The genetic material of most bacteria is organised as a:
options: Linear chromosome paired with histone proteins
questions.explanation: Most bacteria possess one circular, double-stranded DNA chromosome located in the nucleoid, distinct from the linear, histone-associated chromosomes of eukaryotes.

questions.question: Genetic elements such as plasmids that can exist and replicate independently of the main chromosome are called:
questions.explanation: Plasmids, along with some bacteriophage genomes, are extrachromosomal genetic elements that replicate autonomously using their own origin of replication.

questions.question: A plasmid that carries genes enabling it to mediate its own transfer between bacterial cells by conjugation, such as the F plasmid, is called a:
questions.explanation: A conjugative plasmid, such as the F (fertility) plasmid, carries tra genes encoding the machinery (including the sex pilus) needed to transfer itself into a recipient cell.

questions.question: R (resistance) plasmids are of particular medical concern because they:
options: Carry genes conferring resistance to one or more antibiotics and can spread this resistance between bacteria
Encode toxins that directly kill host cells
Are always integrated permanently into the chromosome
Cannot be transferred between bacterial cells
questions.correct_answer: Carry genes conferring resistance to one or more antibiotics and can spread this resistance between bacteria
questions.explanation: R plasmids carry antibiotic-resistance genes and, when conjugative, can transfer multidrug resistance rapidly between bacteria, a major driver of the antimicrobial resistance crisis.

questions.question: DNA replication in bacteria is described as semi-conservative because:
options: Each daughter DNA molecule retains one original (parental) strand and one newly synthesised strand
Both strands of each daughter molecule are entirely new
Both strands of each daughter molecule are entirely from the parent
Only RNA is used as the template
questions.correct_answer: Each daughter DNA molecule retains one original (parental) strand and one newly synthesised strand
questions.explanation: Semi-conservative replication, demonstrated by the Meselson-Stahl experiment, produces two DNA duplexes each composed of one old (template) strand and one newly synthesised strand.

questions.question: The point on the bacterial chromosome at which DNA replication begins is called the:
questions.explanation: Replication in the circular bacterial chromosome initiates at a single, specific site called oriC, from which two replication forks proceed bidirectionally.

questions.question: A permanent, heritable change in the nucleotide sequence of DNA is called a:
questions.explanation: A mutation is any stable, heritable alteration in the DNA sequence, which may arise spontaneously or be induced by physical or chemical mutagens.

questions.question: A mutation in which a single nucleotide base is replaced by a different base is called a:
questions.explanation: A point mutation replaces one base with another; if it changes the encoded amino acid it is a missense mutation, and if it creates a premature stop codon it is a nonsense mutation.

questions.question: Insertion or deletion of a number of nucleotides that is not a multiple of three, shifting the reading frame of a gene, is called a:
questions.explanation: Frameshift mutations alter the reading frame downstream of the insertion or deletion, typically scrambling the encoded protein sequence and often introducing a premature stop codon.

questions.question: A mutation that changes a codon so that it specifies a different amino acid, altering the protein product, is called a:
questions.explanation: A missense mutation is a base substitution that results in a codon for a different amino acid, which may or may not significantly affect protein function depending on the amino acid change.

questions.question: A mutation that changes a sense codon into a premature stop codon, truncating the resulting protein, is called a:
questions.explanation: Nonsense mutations convert an amino acid-coding codon into a stop codon, causing premature termination of translation and typically producing a truncated, non-functional protein.

questions.question: Chemical or physical agents that increase the rate of mutation above the spontaneous background rate are called:
questions.explanation: Mutagens include chemicals (e.g., base analogues, alkylating agents) and physical agents (e.g., UV light, ionising radiation) that damage DNA or interfere with replication, raising mutation frequency.

questions.question: Ultraviolet (UV) radiation is mutagenic mainly because it causes:
options: Formation of pyrimidine (thymine) dimers that distort the DNA helix
Direct breakage of the phosphate backbone only
Insertion of extra nucleotides during replication
questions.correct_answer: Formation of pyrimidine (thymine) dimers that distort the DNA helix
questions.explanation: UV light causes adjacent pyrimidines (commonly thymines) to covalently bond, forming dimers that distort the DNA helix and block normal replication and transcription unless repaired.

questions.question: The DNA repair mechanism that uses photoreactivating enzyme (photolyase) and visible light to directly reverse UV-induced thymine dimers is called:
questions.explanation: Photoreactivation uses the enzyme photolyase, activated by visible light, to directly split thymine dimers and restore the original DNA sequence without removing any nucleotides.

questions.question: A bacterium that requires a specific growth factor not needed by the wild-type (parent) strain, due to a mutation in a biosynthetic gene, is called a/an:
questions.explanation: An auxotroph has lost the ability to synthesise an essential nutrient (e.g., an amino acid or vitamin) due to mutation, and requires it to be supplied in the growth medium, unlike the prototrophic wild type.

questions.question: In the lac operon of E. coli, the operator is the site where:
options: The repressor protein binds to block transcription
RNA polymerase binds to initiate transcription
questions.correct_answer: The repressor protein binds to block transcription
questions.explanation: The operator is a DNA sequence adjacent to the promoter where the lac repressor protein binds in the absence of lactose, physically blocking RNA polymerase from transcribing the structural genes.

questions.question: The lac operon of E. coli is switched on (induced) when:
options: Allolactose binds the repressor, causing it to release the operator
The repressor binds tightly to the operator
questions.correct_answer: Allolactose binds the repressor, causing it to release the operator
questions.explanation: When lactose is available, allolactose (a lactose isomer) binds the lac repressor, changing its conformation so it can no longer bind the operator, allowing RNA polymerase to transcribe the lac genes.

questions.question: A cluster of bacterial structural genes transcribed together as a single mRNA molecule under the control of one promoter is called a/an:
questions.explanation: An operon is a functional unit of coordinately regulated genes (e.g., lac operon: lacZ, lacY, lacA) transcribed as a single polycistronic mRNA from one promoter, a common feature of bacterial gene organisation.

questions.question: The process by which a bacterial cell takes up free (naked) DNA from its environment and incorporates it into its genome is called:
questions.explanation: Transformation involves the uptake of extracellular DNA fragments (e.g., released from lysed cells) by a competent bacterium, followed by recombination into its chromosome or maintenance as a plasmid.

questions.question: A bacterial cell capable of taking up extracellular DNA is described as being:
questions.explanation: Competence is the physiological state, either natural or artificially induced (e.g., by calcium chloride treatment), in which a bacterial cell can take up free DNA from its surroundings.

questions.question: Gene transfer mediated by a bacteriophage that mistakenly packages bacterial DNA instead of (or along with) its own genome and injects it into a new host cell is called:
questions.explanation: In transduction, a bacteriophage accidentally packages host bacterial DNA during assembly and transfers it to a new bacterial cell upon subsequent infection.

questions.question: Generalized transduction, in which any part of the bacterial genome may be transferred, occurs mainly through errors during the:
options: Lytic cycle, when the phage head randomly packages fragments of host DNA
Lysogenic cycle only, with no involvement of the lytic cycle
questions.correct_answer: Lytic cycle, when the phage head randomly packages fragments of host DNA
questions.explanation: During the lytic cycle, host chromosomal DNA is fragmented, and the phage packaging machinery occasionally mispackages a fragment of host DNA instead of phage DNA into a capsid, producing a generalized transducing particle.

questions.question: Specialized transduction differs from generalized transduction in that it:
options: Transfers only specific bacterial genes located adjacent to the prophage's integration site
Can transfer any gene from anywhere on the bacterial chromosome
Does not require a bacteriophage at all
Occurs only through direct cell-to-cell contact
questions.correct_answer: Transfers only specific bacterial genes located adjacent to the prophage's integration site
questions.explanation: Specialized transduction results from imprecise excision of an integrated prophage, which carries with it only the specific host genes flanking its chromosomal attachment site.

questions.question: Bacterial conjugation is a process of gene transfer that requires:
options: Direct cell-to-cell contact, typically via a sex pilus, between a donor and recipient cell
A bacteriophage as an intermediate vector
Uptake of free DNA from the environment
questions.correct_answer: Direct cell-to-cell contact, typically via a sex pilus, between a donor and recipient cell
questions.explanation: Conjugation requires physical contact between an F+ (donor) cell, which extends a sex pilus, and an F- (recipient) cell, through which plasmid or chromosomal DNA is transferred.

questions.question: An Hfr (high frequency of recombination) strain arises when:
options: The F plasmid integrates into the bacterial chromosome
A phage lysogenises the host chromosome
A plasmid is lost from the cell entirely
Two F- cells conjugate with each other
questions.correct_answer: The F plasmid integrates into the bacterial chromosome
questions.explanation: When the F plasmid integrates into the host chromosome by recombination, the resulting Hfr strain can transfer chromosomal genes at high frequency during conjugation, starting from the integration site.

questions.question: Mobile genetic elements that can move from one location to another within or between DNA molecules, sometimes carrying antibiotic-resistance genes, are called:
questions.explanation: Transposons ('jumping genes') are DNA segments that can excise and reinsert themselves at new genomic locations, and composite transposons often carry antibiotic-resistance genes that spread via plasmids.

questions.question: A bacteriophage that integrates its genome into the host chromosome and replicates passively with it, without immediately killing the host cell, is said to be in the:
questions.explanation: In the lysogenic cycle, a temperate phage's DNA (prophage) integrates into the host chromosome and is replicated along with it across generations, until induction triggers entry into the lytic cycle.

questions.question: A bacterial cell carrying an integrated, dormant prophage is referred to as:
questions.explanation: A lysogenic (or lysogen) bacterium harbours a prophage integrated into its chromosome; the prophage is replicated with the host DNA and can later be induced to enter the lytic cycle.

questions.question: Genetic recombination between homologous DNA sequences, which can integrate transferred DNA into the recipient chromosome, is primarily catalysed in bacteria by the protein:
questions.explanation: RecA protein mediates homologous recombination by promoting strand exchange between similar DNA sequences, enabling incoming DNA from transformation, transduction, or conjugation to integrate into the recipient chromosome.

questions.question: In the Griffith transformation experiment with Streptococcus pneumoniae, mice injected with a mixture of heat-killed virulent (S) bacteria and live avirulent (R) bacteria died because:
options: A 'transforming principle' from the dead S bacteria converted some live R bacteria into virulent S bacteria
The heat-killed bacteria spontaneously became alive again
The R bacteria were virulent on their own
Mice are always killed by any bacterial injection
questions.correct_answer: A 'transforming principle' from the dead S bacteria converted some live R bacteria into virulent S bacteria
questions.explanation: Griffith's 1928 experiment showed that genetic material released from heat-killed virulent S strain bacteria could transform live avirulent R strain bacteria into virulent S strain bacteria, later identified by Avery, MacLeod and McCarty as DNA.

questions.question: In bacterial genetics, a wild-type gene that has reverted from a mutant phenotype back to the original (or a functionally similar) phenotype has undergone:
questions.explanation: A reverse mutation (reversion) restores the original wild-type phenotype, either by exactly reversing the original mutation or by a second, compensatory mutation elsewhere (suppressor mutation).
